#3822. Old School RuneScape Is Following World Of Warcraft: Classic And Adding A Permadeath Hardcore Mode

Today, Jagex announced that its live version of original RuneScape, called Old School RuneScape, is getting a new game mode that will be familiar to fans of other MMORPGs: hardcore mode.

In hardcore, you only get one life. Once you die, your character is dead, and the only way you can keep playing is by starting a new character. Everything else is the same, including future content and updates to Old School RuneScape.

When characters die in hardcore OSRS, the Grim Reaper appears and offers the player a choice. They can either fully reset their progress and start over from level 1, or they can keep everything they’ve done and move their character into the main game to keep playing outside of hardcore. All items that are not considered “items kept on death” will be lost.

To access hardcore, just boot up OSRS: hardcore is present as a new type of realm you can make a character on. The mode is available today across all platforms: PC, iOS, and Android. As someone who has diedÂ an awful lot in RuneScape over the years, I’m interested to see how this impacts the experience. Suddenly, it’s far more risky to wander into high-level areas to chop wood, or to head down to the scorpion pit to mine ore. The trailer even depicts cows and low-level goblins as a concern.

RuneScape is following in the footsteps of World of Warcraft here, which added hardcore servers to World of Warcraft: Classic back in 2023. This game mode works roughly the same as RuneScape‘s version: game’s the same, no revival on death, can transfer to other realms after you die. These servers haveÂ been a massive hit among the Classic community, so much so they’re coming to World of Warcraft: Forever sometime after launch as well. Funnily enough, Forever also launches on November 4, though it won’t have hardcore right away. It’s a busy week in the MMOs.

#3821. The Division 2 Y8S3 Red Horizon Climax mission walkthrough

The Climax mission for Y8S3 Red Horizon is now available in The Division 2, and it’s your guaranteed shot at an Exotic. Once unlocked, you can then complete the mission at Master to guarantee yourself the Loaded for Bear Exotic gloves.

To unlock the mission, complete the three Scout challenges in Y8S3 that feature HVTs. You can also complete the remaining Scout weeks, but that’s completely optional. Once unlocked, head to the Washington National Airport to begin the mission.

Wait for the cutscene to play out, as Manny will provide you with the starting instructions. Your first task is to help the militia stuck at the clinic. The marker will directly lead you to the room where a few militia members are stuck.

Kill all the enemies you find at the location. There will be two waves of enemies, with a few elite ones to take down. They will fire at you from all sides, so be careful about incoming damage.

Once you clear all the enemies, your next task is to rendezvous with Avery Miles. Follow the marker to reach Avery and protect the NPC from all incoming damage. There will be several enemies to take down, and they will all primarily focus their shots towards Avery. Your best option is to kill the enemies after intercepting them.

Once the remaining Cleaners are killed, you can proceed to the next step. Follow the marker to reach the Hangar, and there will be plenty of enemies to kill. Since the fight takes place in an open area, use the fence coverings as much as possible.

Once you take care of the cleaners, you’ll need to disable two fuel pumps. The pumps are on either side of the deconstructed aircraft in the middle. You can just trace them by their pipes. However, focus first on the enemies since that will make things easier for you.

Keep proceeding through the airport and clear the incoming enemies until you get the objective to secure the concourse. Then, reach the tarmac to sabotage the pumps. Keep killing the enemies until the objective marker pops up to disclose the pump locations.

Finally, Bobby Guzman will appear. He is the main enemy of this Climax mission, and he will be a hard challenge. He has plenty of armor on him, and he is surrounded by other elite enemies.

Finally, a timer will commence, giving you approximately a minute to escape. Do so safely, and you’ll successfully finish the Climax mission. You get the guaranteed Exotic drop by playing at Master. Anything less means obtaining the Exotic will be luck-dependent.

#3820. Silent Hill: Townfall adds new Hard difficulty in latest update

Silent Hill: Townfall has added a new Hard difficulty mode and rebalanced every existing setting to make room for it.

The update, patch 1.6.0, went live on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store earlier this week, according to patch notes published by Konami. Konami said the rebalance is designed to create "a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from".

As part of that rebalance, resources have been adjusted in some sections of the game, and enemies' hearing now gets sharper as the difficulty level goes up. Your position is now visible on the map in whichever mode you pick, while the reduction to the main enemy's attack severity now applies only in Story Mode.

Anyone who picks Nightmare for their first playthrough will now see a warning screen. The difficulty selection menu also gives a clearer summary of how the options differ.

SILENT HILL: TownfallNotice: Game Update (Patch 1.6.0)An update tuning gameplay and addressing some in-game issues is now available.Please check that the version number in the lower right corner of the main menu is displayed as v1.6.155963.*The PlayStation®5 version is…

The update also improves the valve status lighting for colourblind players, adds more hints and tutorials, and tweaks the wording of some puzzle hints and items. The options menu has been reorganised into clearer categories, and the controls remapping option has been renamed to make it clear that keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too, not just controllers.

PC players also get a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option, alongside the usual general improvements and bug fixes.

To check you're on the latest version, look for v1.6.155963 in the lower right corner of the main menu on PC, or v1.6.156035 on PS5.

Developed by Screen Burn and published by Konami, Silent Hill: Townfall launched on PS5 and PC on 24th September. Matt said Townfall showed Silent Hill's "stellar revival continues as new developer Screen Burn melds stealth, meticulous world design, and a dash of social realism for a different sort of survival horror", and awarded it four out of five stars in Eurogamer's Silent Hill: Townfall review.

The first trailer for Lords of War, a direct sequel to Nicolas Cage's 2005 crime thriller Lord of War, has arrived with Bill Skarsgard in tow.

Per the film's official synopsis, the movie sees Yuri (Cage) reunite with his son Orlov (Skarsgard), but as Orlov tries to right his father's wrongs rather than stop them he launches a mercenary army to fight America's Middle East conflicts. In the trailer, which can be viewed above, it doesn't seem like a happy father-son reunion as Orlov spends most of the brief clip chasing his father around with a gun.

Andrew Niccol returns to direct from a script he once again penned himself. The cast includes Laura Harrier, Sylvia Hoeks, and Greg Tarzan Davis.

The original film, inspired by the real-life events of Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout, premiered in 2005 to mixed-to-positive reviews, but failed to perform at the global box office. The cast includes Hawke, Jared Leto, Bridget Moynahan, Sammi Rotibi, Ian Holm, and Eamonn Walker.

A sequel was announced back in 2023, with Niccol excitedly stating: "There is so much more to explore with these characters. Plato said it best – 'Only the dead have seen the end of war.'" He also noted that Orlov is Yuri's "illegitimate son," but I guess we'll just have to watch the movie in order to find out what that means...

Lords of War hits theaters on January 22, 2027. For more, check out our list of all the exciting upcoming movies in 2026 and beyond.

The Taiwanese semiconductor and non-volatile memory manufacturer Macronix is phasing out its ROM production, according to its CEO and chairman, Miin Wu. Thatâs potentially terrible news for fans of physical games, as Macronix is Nintendoâs main ROM supplier for Nintendo Switch cartridges.

During the presentation, Macronix CEO Miin Wu revealed that the company had enjoyed a ârecord-highâ net profit of roughly $337 million for its Q3 2026 period. But in a translation provided by the Taipei Times, Wu stated that Macronixâs customersâ âdemand for NOR used in data centersâ was primarily the source of its record-high profits, while also noting that its ROM sales had dwindled by a whopping 39 percent over the past year.

1/4 Nintendo's main memory chip maker is quitting the Switch businessMacronix, which makes the ROM chips in Switch 1 and Switch 2 game memory cards, is phasing out that business. There will be no new ROM products, and Q3 is the last quarter it reports ROM sales separately.

As ROM chip sales only made up five percent of Macronixâs sales in Q3 2026, down from 26 percent in Q2 2025, Wu stated that the company has already begun gradually phasing out ROM production in favor of delivering âmore NOR flash solutions for data centersâ and âallocating capacity to NAND, a high-growth segment that will drive Macronixâs long-term expansion.â

As Gibson noted, digital Nintendo Switch sales now make up â61.5 percent of Nintendo’s software salesâ as of April to June 2026, an increase of 2.2 percent when compared to Nintendoâs year-on-year sales at the end of 2025.

#3816. Final Fantasy 14 reveals Evercold’s second new job and February release date, with pre-orders opening next week

Plus Square Enix confirms Final Fantasy 14 has passed 35m registered accounts.

Final Fantasy 14's next expansion, Evercold, will launch on 23rd February 2027, and its second new job is zephyr, a physical ranged DPS that fights with a crossbow and a bird.

Producer and director Naoki Yoshida revealed the job during the opening keynote of the Final Fantasy 14 Fan Festival 2026 in Tokyo. Zephyr pairs crossbow shots with support from an avian familiar called Nephele, and joins Bastion, the greatshield-wielding tank revealed as Evercold's first new job at Fan Festival Berlin earlier this year.

Pre-orders for Evercold and the previously announced Collector's Box open on Wednesday 4th November at 9am GMT. Anyone who pre-orders gets early access, plus a Wind-Up Köttr minion and Halone's Earring, which boosts EXP from defeating enemies by 30 percent. The in-game items are delivered as soon as you pre-order, so you can use the earring to level jobs before Evercold arrives.

The Collector's Box is physical goods only. It doesn't include the game, in-game items or pre-order bonuses. Inside you'll find an art box featuring an Evercold illustration by Yoshitaka Amano, a figure of the Warrior of Light as a reaper, an Ethos metal keychain, a Köttr mini plush, and a Tapestry of the Fourth.

The Square Enix Store is also selling a limited Collector's Bundle that pairs the box with a code for the Digital Collector's Edition on Windows or Mac. Players on PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and Steam can buy the box on its own and pre-order the Digital Collector's Edition separately. The digital edition adds a Valhallar Odin mount, an Entreat Crystal emote, and a Crystal Skyltborg weapon for Bastion.

Square Enix also used the keynote to reveal a new Fierce raid difficulty, sitting between Normal and Savage; a new trailer for the Evangelion: Ghosts of Desire alliance raid crossover, plus tougher eight-player battles built around some of its bosses; and new Tetsuya Nomura artwork for Beyond the Lifestream, a raid series crossover with the Final Fantasy 7 Remake series.

We can also expect Evolved Combat Mode, which Square Enix says highlights each job's unique identity; Seasons, a new system that changes how item rewards are earned; and expanded character creation with new Character Action Skins. Expanded housing features, PvP updates, and a revamped companion chocobo system will follow from patch 8.1.

Final Fantasy 14 has passed 35 million registered accounts.

You can watch the full keynote on Twitch, and there's more on the official Evercold site.

Final Fantasy 14 is now available on Switch 2. The port was announced at the end of June.

The long-awaited title of the next Elder Scrolls game was revealed in a video marking Bethesda Softworks' 40th anniversary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eight years after it was announced, it's finally officially official: The next RPG in Bethesda's long-running Elder Scrolls series is called Sentinel.

The title was revealed in a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, narrated by Todd Howard (of course), who cast back to the studio's first game, Gridiron—Bethesda was big on sports games back in the day—before moving into The Elder Scrolls series, the games that would take it to the big leagues, in the early 1990s.

"As we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Howard says as the video draws to an end.

"And so even though yes, we're looking back,we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

And thus is the title revealed: Sentinel.

There's an interesting quote after the title is revealed: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." Those words were uttered by Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell in the year 4E 206, which was UESP pointed out puts Sentinel at least five years after the events of Skyrim.

No other details are revealed, but the title (and that quote) presumably also reveals the setting: Hammerfell, home of the redguards. Sentinel itself is one of Hammerfell's major kingdoms and capital of the Alik'r Desert—reflected in the teaser's sandy backdrop. It's something of a geographical shift from the flyover of the generic mountains seen in that 2018 reveal, although the Alik'r is bordered by the Dragontail Mountains, so who knows.

So there you have it! The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Hopefully it won't take another eight years before we hear anything more about it.

#3814. Sam Altman Pulls Spectacular 180 After Unpopular Comments About RAM: ‘It Is F*cking Annoying’

During a recent podcast appearance, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made everyone mad by explaining that it was “terrible” that people wanted to have RAM in their own computers. Instead, he suggested, the limited supply of memory should be used in data centers powering AI services and tools. People didn’t like those comments, and now Altman is claiming that’s not what he meant at all.

On November 3, right in the middle of a massive blue wave that swept across the country during election night, Altman replied with “I LOL’d’ to a joke image featuring RAM sticks leading up to a box trap. In response, someone joked he should rename himself to Ram Altman on Twitter, which he agreed to do, but not because he wants to consume all the memory in the world for his own data centers. Instead, it’s because he wants everyone to know that he really wants them all to have their own RAM. And he’s not happy that people allegedly took his comments out of context to paint him as some RAM-hoarding bad guy.

“I actually do want the world to have tons of memory and people to put as much as they want in their computers,” said Ram Altman on Twitter. “And it is fucking annoying that this was taken out of context. I have been arguing for the world to ramp up memory production for a long time.”

Let’s go back to Altman’s original quote from last week. Here it is in case you forgot:

But from a global allocation perspective, actually, itâs quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the worldâs limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time. You want maximum utilization in the cloud if youâre trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow everyoneâsâmany peopleâs intuition is the opposite of that.

Hmmm, the quote above really does make it seem like Altman isn’t a fan of people having RAM in their computers, as he and other tech giants struggle to build data centers and buy up memory. Though, to be fair, Altman’s original comment does mention limited supply being a factor.

Though, hey, I wonder why RAM is so limited right now? Oh right, it’s because AI hyperscalers and big tech have been buying up all the memory they can get their hands on, making it harder for companies like Valve and Nintendo to build new hardware while driving up costs for everyone. So yeah, I bet Altman wants memory production to ramp up, but I don’t think it’s because he wants the PlayStation 6 to be more affordable.

#3812. Activision to remove Itaewon crowd crush footage from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and apologises to victims' families

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims."

Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

In a new statement reported by Inven Global, Activision said the footage "will be completely removed" via a game update scheduled to roll out on 12th November.

The statement was issued in Korean, and the quotes come via Inven Global's AI-assisted, editor-reviewed translation.

As we reported earlier this week, the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died. The bereaved families' association and the Citizens Countermeasure Meeting called for its removal.

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims who were deeply hurt by this incident, as well as to everyone we have caused concern," Activision said.

The publisher also said that Modern Warfare 4 "is a work of fiction created to provide realistic immersion", and it "never intended to evoke or trivialise any tragic event, including the Itaewon crowd crush" by using real news broadcast footage.

The controversy has also reached the South Korean government. During a press briefing, minister of the interior and safety Yun Ho-jung described the footage's inclusion as "secondary harm", and said: "I believe appropriate sanctions should be imposed".

"Using such a tragedy as material for a game, a form of entertainment or business, is something that should be refrained from as a matter of human ethics," Yun added. He said it was up to the relevant agencies to decide "whether to impose punishment or block it to make general access difficult".

Activision's earlier statement to Eurogamer said the opening cinematic "utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative", and was "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".

World of Warcraft's big crossover with Dungeons & Dragons is finally here—and despite being a huge flagship collaboration, one of the biggest MMOs meeting with one of the biggest TTRPGs, I'm sad to say I'm feeling just a touch whelmed. This sourcebook is inconsistent—filled with very cool character options in some places, and just pointing at the already-existing player's handbook in others.

That inconsistency doesn't let the whole project down, mind. There are still some rules tucked away in here that I think are great additions to any campaign, not just a World of Warcraft-themed one.

Let's start with the big one: Classes. WoW and D&D do have a lot of overlap in terms of class fantasy—there's not much in the way of appreciable differences between a Fighter and a Warrior, other than a few iconic abilities being missing from the pack. As a result, this rulebook essentially uses the pre-existing classes as a template to throw some WoW flavour on.

Some of these changes are meaningful—take, for example, the Death Knight. This uses the Paladin's chassis, but throws in a ton of impactful changes, replacing Lay on Hands with Death Coil, for example. It also throws a whole new raft of Death Knight-adjacent spells, adjusts your Find Steed with a cool undead ghost that can phase through objects, and more.

A lot of the classes are solved by custom spells like this—the Paladin, for instance, has just the one new subclass to cover for Holy and a bunch of iconic Paladin spells. But the balance of these is a touch skewiff in places. Take Divine Shield, for instance. This thing is straight busted.

It's a 4th level spell, which does admittedly mean you'll only get it at levels 13 plus, but it makes you immune to not only the damage of a triggering attack, but also all damage until the start of your next turn. AND you can't be moved or have your speed reduced. While absolutely correct for the flavour of WoW's iconic bubble, this is crazy overpowered.

And while some of these classes do have a lot new on offer, others are so thin on content it's a wonder why they're there at all. The rogue gets a particularly short end of the stick, for instance. Outlaw rogues are just given a reskinned version of 5e's Swashbuckler subclass (which does, in fairness, have some new Cunning Strike options to bring it up to parity). Otherwise, the book just points you in the direction of pre-existing subclasses.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Others are a complete miss, too. Shamans are all awkwardly stuffed into the chassis of the Barbarian, which only really works for Enhancement shamans—Elemental and Restoration shamans are pretty much just your standard D&D barbarian with some flavour-adjacent rage options, rather than the full spellcasters they are in the videogame.

This inconsistency in quality applies to character origins, too. Some of them have fully bespoke traits—Dracthyr get their visage forms, Void Elves get this cool void form that triggers when you hit identical numbers on an Advantage/Disadvantage roll, and so on. And then there are Orcs and Dwarves, some of WoW's most iconic races, where the book goes: Just use the stuff that's already in the PHB.

And yet, there's a lot to this supplement I actually like. When it's actually adding new options to the classes, I think they're cool—the Frost Mage flavoured feat, Fingers of Frost, gives you extra cold damage against restrained creatures, for example. But the real thing I would encourage you to just crib for your non-Azerothian games are its gathering and crafting systems.

In 5e (and the 2024 rules), crafting's always been sort of a joke. There are tool proficiencies, but they might come up every once in a blue moon. The actual Player's Handbook just says to half the cost of an item, then smacks you around the head with a massive downtime cost for anything particularly expensive—a suit of plate armor takes a whopping 150 days to craft (though you can split this with extra help). At which point you might as well just eat the GP cost and buy the damn thing.

This book, however, has some really neat rules for gathering and crafting professions. Having the right tool proficiency gives you access to a profession, which you can level up when your proficiency bonus increases to new tiers (which also increases the rarity of the items you can make).

Instead of making players shell out the gold cost, these gathering professions have a neat little table for getting enough golds' worth in raw materials to make the thing, with extra bonuses for beating the involved DC by five or more. When you get to higher levels, certain recipes might require items from specific regions—and you might only know how to make those items via recipes obtained from certain factions.

It's still all pretty lightweight (although each profession does have a useful list of suggested recipes it should know) but that's honestly a boon to this system, rather than a bane, because you could very easily just slot this whole mechanic into your homebrew campaign with very little trouble.

And, more to the point, you could very easily make entire adventure hooks out of going to get specific materials for a recipe here—which helps solve D&D crafting's main issue: It's not relevant unless you have literal months of in-game downtime to kill. While the book doesn't make changes to the time-to-craft issue, it's still a major step up.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent."

Renown's another mechanic I like. You get renown with certain factions based on your origins, but you can increase this renown through play to get certain perks. For instance, improved renown with Darnassus gives you the option to learn certain proficiencies, gain a blessing from its leaders, or gather extra materials with herbalism. My favorite of these is the gnomeregan Shield Guardian perk, which specifically states that if you dip below 50 renown again, the guardian turns on you. Sorry buddy, my creator says you dropped off.

Aside from these rules additions, there are also some solid dungeon adventures with their own bespoke stat blocks, extra magic items, and a respectable bestiary full of critters to toss into your campaign.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent—some areas have novel, if a little wonky, additions to the system. Others shrug like the book's designers simply ran out of time and budget, pointing towards resources that you already own.

However, if you are looking to run a WoW-specific campaign, or just want crafting rules that don't suck, it very well might be worth checking out on the strength of its secondary mechanics alone. Just don't go in there expecting a 1:1 replication of the MMORPG. This is still Dungeons & Dragons—and in some places, I mean that literally.

#3805. How to collect Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

Fortnite’s Treasure Hunters season has quite a few different One Piece-themed missions available for you to tackle. One of the first ones you’ll encounter tasks you with collecting Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them.

The loot pool is massive, so figuring out how to find any specific item around the island can be tricky. If this task is giving you trouble, here’s how to collect Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them in Fortnite.

Nami’s Tangerines are a random loot drop item you can find just about anywhere on the island while looting. There is no specific, guaranteed way to find them, which means you instead have to regularly loot and hope you eventually come across them.

You have a chance of finding Nami’s Tangerines when opening any loot container you come across while exploring. This includes:

You can also find Nami’s Tangerines sitting on the ground anywhere around the island. They’re fairly common, so once you’re actively looking for them, finding the total amount required for this mission should be fairly easy.

Each time you come across Nami’s Tangerines, you’ll generally find more than one. Typically, they come in bundles of around three. This helps you progress through the mission associated with them much faster, as you need to find quite a few of them to get it done.

To complete the collect Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them quest, you need to find a total of 16 Nami’s Tangerines around the island. You don’t actually have to eat them; instead, you simply need to pick them up and have them in your inventory briefly for them to count toward this task.

You can find all 16 Nami’s Tangerines in one match or instead slowly work your way through this task across a few different ones. All that matters for this mission is that you eventually do manage to collect a total of 16 at some point before the season ends.

Macronix is pivoting to supply AI data centers, but the company isn't making Switch 2 cartridges anyway

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Macronix, the manufacturer Nintendo relies on to make Switch 1 cartridges, is phasing out production of the chips that power those games. That certainly sounds like another blow to physical media, and it may well be, but as it stands this news is unlikely to affect cartridges for Switch 2.

Macronix reports record profits in its latest quarterly financial period, and according to chairman Miin Wu, it does not expect to be able to expand its manufacturing capacity in order to fuel further growth. "Instead, near-term growth will be driven primarily by price increases," Wu says, as reported by Taipei Times.

Switch cartridges are powered by flash memory, which is the same type of tech that AI data centers are now eagerly gobbling at massively inflated prices. Chip manufacturers have found that they can make a lot more money selling their goods to data centers rather than makers of consumer electronics, leading to the global memory shortages that have presented us with the threat of next-gen consoles costing $1,000 or more.

Wu notes that demand for the chips "used in data centers is very robust," which is why it's emphasizing those while phasing out production of ROM chips, which are the ones that power Switch game cartridges.

However, Macronix does not manufacture Switch 2 cartridges – at least as far as we know. Details on Nintendo's manufacturing partners are poorly reported, but teardowns suggest that Switch 2 cartridges are primarily made by a separate company called Rohm, as well as another, unidentified manufacturer.

As noted by Nintendo Patents Watch, Macronix had apparently been trying to enter the Switch 2 cartridge business, but has seemingly never completed the R&D work necessary to get the ball rolling. If Macronix had entered the space, it might've opened the door to cheaper or higher-capacity physical Switch 2 games, which may have swayed some publishers away from game-key cards.

But that's pure speculation. As it stands, Macronix's exit from the ROM business won't affect the Switch 2 cartridge market. The effect on Switch 1 games is more difficult to measure, since that market is shrinking anyway – Nintendo itself has no more Switch 1 games on the horizon, though boutique publishers continue to put out physical games for the system.

Nintendo has recently reiterated that it has "no plans to ditch physical games," and it doesn't seem there's any reason to expect that to change with Macronix's pivot.

#3802. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake review – Remasterpiece

An all-time classic reborn respectfully and beautifully.

I’ve talked in the past about how I’m not particularly a fan of the Zelda games, but it’s mostly because I’ve just never really dived into them, especially the latest open-world ones. But for Ocarina of Time, I’ve dabbled many times before and always respected it for how much it’s loved, even if I never could quite grasp the excitement myself.

As a kid, I remembered feeling overwhelmed and annoyed with the game’s controls (especially on that cumbersome Nintendo 64 controller) and muddy framerate that even then made it feel like a slog. Thankfully, with the newest version for Nintendo Switch 2, all of those issues have been assuaged to create a genuine masterpiece, reborn for modern-day gamers.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is genuinely one of the best games I’ve ever played, and one that I think all players of all ages should experience, whether they’re a hardcore fan of the original or a newcomer going in with zero knowledge. It’s just that good.

It all starts with a boy in the forest, a chosen one of sorts, who is shockingly thrust into an exciting, adorable journey to meet a princess and save the world. From there, from what I’ve gathered, it’s the same timeless story you remember from 1998. I venture to guess that long-time fans of this game will have a very emotional experience reliving it

At its heart, Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 is what I would call a respectful remake/remaster, even if many will probably feel like Nintendo played it a bit too safe this time around. The changes made here have been minimal, focusing on quality-of-life improvements like the game’s controls, visuals, and sound, to enhance the experience without changing it very much at all.

Remakes are always a tricky task, because you need to maintain the allure of the original while also making it worthwhile to play a second time around. There’s been two kinds of remakes in recent years: games like Resident Evil 4 or Final Fantasy VII, which reshape the story and gameplay in numerous ways, or Metal Gear Solid Delta: Snake Eater and Demon’s Souls, which stay very true to the original, while focusing more on modernization and quality-of-life. Ocarina of Time definitely falls into the latter.

At the outset, the beauty of modern tech and the Switch 2’s hardware is on full display, boasting some of the best visuals the new console has released yet, especially when it comes to adding details that were not possible on N64: interiors look different thanks to no longer being flat polygons, Link’s tunics have awesome designs in the fabric, and even change color when it gets wet. And then there’s little things, how Link’s mouth subtly opens when taking a breath between notes on the Ocarina (you can also play the songs in the game by humming into your Switch 2, which is just plain cool).

It’s all incredibly detailed and gorgeous, and it’s locked at a rock-solid 60 FPS throughout, creating a smooth experience that we could’ve only ever dreamed of when dealing with the 20-FPS slog the original game offered.

Putting another of my complaints about the original to rest, the controls have been reimagined for modern games and gamers, and are incredibly well optimized for the Switch 2, especially when it comes to the Pro Controller (my preferred method whenever possible). Link can now sprint, and there’s a dedicated button for jumping, making platforming sections a joy. And yes, even the Water Temple is way better now, with the ability to quickly equip and unequip the Iron Boots by pressing down on the D-pad.

The hero can now also target foes with the ZL button and lock onto them when close, making combat a breeze, and maybe even a bit too easy, with nary a real challenge in my 25-plus hours in a first run, even with the game’s awesome and memorable boss fights. I couldn’t help but feel a bit of the adventure’s age here, so it would’ve been cool to see the combat maybe tweaked a bit to bring more of a challenge, but I don’t think it’s a huge deal either way.

This still feels like a masterclass in level design and gradual progression, all these years later. There’s no XP to earn, no checklists, just gradually getting stronger and unlocking new items to help you reach new heights on your journey, with some minor side quests to get into along the way.

Other additions to the adventure for 2026 include Threads of Time, which is a tapestry that weaves Link’s story as you play it, but also serves as a bit of a quest log if you don’t know where to go next. This is very helpful considering there are a ton of side quests, collectibles, and minor interactions to find both in the open world and dungeons you must conquer.

You can easily learn where to go or what to do by talking to NPCs around the vast kingdom of Hyrule, but the tapestry will occasionally update with an objective that you can finish (or not) by gently pushing you in a direction. For me, it was nice to have, considering I don’t remember much about the original game.

There’s also the Hall of Fallen Foes, which is a menagerie of enemies you’ve defeated that you unlock in the later stages of the game. It serves as something of a museum, allowing to to walk around and view the models of monsters and enemies you’ve taken down, but also do battle with them again to reprise the boss fights at your leisure.

The other main difference in this version of the game is the addition of voice acting in certain cutscenes. Many of the game’s conversations are done through text dialogue, but big story beats are voice-acted by a number of important characters like Navi, the Great Deku Tree, Zelda, and of course, Ganon. Everyone here sounds great, which is easy for me to say because I haven’t had my own version of their voices in my head for a few decades like long-time fans will. But don’t worry, the silent protagonist stays silent here, too, other than his classic grunts and exclamations while exerting himself.

The changes made to Ocarina of Time feel meaningful and worthwhile, and they do nothing to detract from the original game’s legendary experience. Instead, they enhance it in every way, making an unforgettable journey more accessible and fun than it ever has been.

I got a little emotional while playing OoT on Switch 2, especially when using the Ocarina to travel to and from the past. How jealous I am of Link’s ability to travel back in time. Like Link, I first entered the Temple of Time as a child and returned as an adult. Much has changed in the 28 years since the original was released, but the charm of this game is still there, and it feels prevalent throughout, even with a “modern” art style and rerecorded musical score.

I will leave a word of warning, however: make multiple saves before heading to the last areas of the game to take on the final boss, if you want to reach 100 percent completion and take on all the game has to offer. There’s no New Game Plus option, and no real option to go back and complete things if you don’t have a separate file ready to go (I’d be happy to find out I missed something if I’m wrong here).

I’d like to close with saying that, in my professional life as a journalist and critic, I’ve always felt hesitant to give out a score like this. It’s not perfect (nothing and no game is), but I’m confident that this is the one game to break that personal barrier with. Ocarina of Time is a legendary experience for a reason, and this remake is one of the best of its kind I’ve played yet. I’m hopeful that longtime fans will enjoy it, and I know that newcomers will find a lot of fun in the franchise if they’re diving in for the first time.

#3801. Dune: Awakening's free Blood and Ice expansion swaps sand for snow on 1st December

Funcom's survival MMO Dune: Awakening is heading north with a free expansion that trades the deserts of Arrakis for a frozen new map.

The expansion, called Blood and Ice, will release on 1st December. Funcom said it adds "around 35 hours of new progression", along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialisation traits. It's coming to PC, PS5, and Xbox.

The new map, called the Polar Sink, turns the game's usual survival loop upside down. Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm, upgrading your gear with resources found only in the Polar Sink.

The map is split into two biomes, the tundra and the ice cap. You'll start in the tundra, where wealthy water shipper families have built lavish strongholds, before trying to get into the heavily guarded ice cap. Once you're in, you can harvest ice to cool your base equipment and speed up production.

According to Funcom, the expansion "brings the focus back to ground-level survival, with traversal, temperature management, and combat all playing important roles in your progression". The studio also said future updates will add more reasons to go back to the region.

Blood and Ice also brings a new Events tab to the main menu. Shortly after the expansion launches, a new event called Water Crisis will follow the current one, The Scourge. Funcom says every event can be completed in both single-player and multiplayer, and that it plans to run them more often, each with new stories and free rewards.

Funcom has also launched a cosmetics store, which it says will help fund continued development and free updates. The store will start with a rotating selection of items, including looks taken from the Dune films to coincide with Dune: Part Three's release in cinemas this December. The plan is to eventually make the full catalogue available at all times.

Several of the community's most-requested features are also on the way. Offline single-player is due this month, and from January 2027 you'll be able to copy characters from multiplayer servers to single-player, and from single-player to select private or self-hosted servers on PC. Full cross-play will also arrive in January 2027.

"We're far from done," Funcom said, adding that it has "ambitious plans for the year ahead", including major free updates in 2027. The studio says more than a million new players have joined since the game launched on consoles, alongside a rebuilt endgame, three DLCs, and the conclusion of the game's first story arc, Book One.

Just a couple of weeks ago, Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - confirmed it was entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening.

#3800. The Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Has No Master Quest

Master QuestRemakeSwitch 2The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is out November 5 in the U.S. and already live for millions of Switch 2 owners in New Zealand and other parts of the world. The good news is that the early reviews have been absolutely glowing for Nintendo’s latest exclusive. The bad news is that they’ve also confirmed there’s no much-requested Master Quest mode.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Master QuestÂ was a reworked version of the N64 game that made it much harder. It was released for the GameCube in 2003 in limited quantities around the launch of Wind Waker. Extremely rare but extremely rewarding for hardcore Ocarina of Time fans who knew the original game like the back of their hands, it functioned as a callback to the more difficult Second Quest for the first Zelda on NES. It was part of the Ocarina of Time remaster on 3DS, too.

As a result, many were hoping Nintendo would include some version of Master Quest mode in the Ocarina of Time remake on Switch 2. According to those who have already finished the game, however, there’s no such option here. “It honestly bums me out that the remake doesnât include a sort of Hero Mode, or even better, the Master Quest variant for veteran Heroes of Time to make us sweat a little too,” Scott White and Alex Donaldson wrote for RPGSite.

Anna Koselke, in her review for Gamesradar, was similarly disappointed. “There’s no Master Quest version to play through,” she wrote. “So, for the time being, my journey with the Ocarina of Time remake ends. I’m sent back to the menu screen that still lives rent-free in my head, left wishing I could explore more of this take on Nintendo’s gem, or at least enjoy it once more without losing the mark of my previous progress.”

Nintendo hasn’t been shy about delivering free content updates for its Switch 2 games. Star Fox recently received new multiplayer content, and Mario Kart 8 Deluxe even received an entire new 8-player split-screen mode on the newer hardware. It’s easy to imagine a Master Quest mode, or at least a new game+ option, being added to Ocarina of Time in the months ahead, even if it’s not clear what would stop that from being included in the base game from the jump.

While players can access the original version of Ocarina of Time on Switch Online, the Master Quest add-on remains absent there as well. Maybe it’ll be added to the GameCube’s growing library on Switch 2 at some point.

Konami might have finally set down the Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol 1 to focus on releasing Metal Gear Solid 4 from its PS3 prison, but modders continue chipping away at the PS2-and-earlier era Metal Gear games. MGSHDFix, whose mission statement is to repair broken visual bugs, fix crashes, and generally give the older Metal Gears a bit of a spitshine, has got a big new update. Now is the era of MGSHDFix 5.0 (actually, 5.0.1. There was a hotfix).

"We've got performance improvements, massive vanilla loading time reductions for MGS2, loose .MP3/.WAV/.OGG/FLAC soundtrack loading for MG1/MG2, WIP raw mouse input support, and loads of new restoration and bugfixes", writes author Afevis Solmunko.

There are, to be honest, way too many fixes to properly delve into here, so I recommend either checking the patch notes out yourself or taking the mod for a spin in your preferred Metal Gear. We can call out some of the big ones, though.

For example, want to play Metal Gear 2 as Mel Gibson? No? Well that's a shame, bucko, because MGSHDFix 5.0 provides an option to restore that game's MSX2 sprites. "Yes, you can finally experience Mel Gibson fighting Sean Connery as Kojima intended," writes Solmunko.

Also in the OG MGs, there's now an option "to make doors automatically check your inventory for keycards (how MGS2 keycards work)", which frankly sounds blasphemous to me.

More practically, the latest version of the mod boasts that it dramatically cuts down loading times in MGS2. "We've greatly sped up level loading by adding a new system that prefetches a list of all the assets for all the rooms that are directly connected to the current stage you're in… Speedrunners have reported that this new prefetch system has shaved upwards to 5 minutes off of the elapsed realtime from their runs". On Linux (and thus, Steam Deck) specifically, Solmunko says this can "reduce level transitions load times by 4~6 seconds for every room you go into".

Plus, MGS2 and MGS3 now have limited support for raw mouse input in third-person, with support for first-person hopefully coming in MGSHDFix 5.1.0.

#3798. How to get Captain X rewards in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

There are many unique skins you can unlock in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. One of the toughest ones to get your hands on is Captain X, a battle pass Outfit that requires quite a bit of progression to obtain.

This style will only be around and available to earn through quests in this season, so if you’re interested in adding it to your collection, you’ve got to get to work on it fast. Since Treasure Hunters is a mini-season, you’ve got quite a limited amount of time to work on it, so here’s how to get Captain X and all of his rewards in Fortnite.

Captain X is the grand prize in the Captain X rewards series, which means you must fully work through this special set of missions to earn him. To progress in this series, you need to complete varying amounts of weekly tasks. A total of 24 weekly quests must be finished to unlock him.

While there are lots of free rewards up for grabs this season, like Solid Gold A$AP Rocky and other rewards in the Pirate Chest, Captain X is not one of them. He is a battle pass-only outfit, which means you must have this pass unlocked to progress toward earning him.

Captain X also cannot be unlocked early on in the season, as there aren’t enough missions available to complete for him. He won’t be obtainable until Nov. 21, close to the very end of Treasure Hunters.

To ensure you’re able to get him, though, you’ll want to keep on top of completing as many weekly quests as possible leading up to his unlock date. Fresh missions are added every week, and checking off as many of them as possible will ensure you’re able to unlock Captain X and all of his associated prizes as soon as it’s possible to do so.

In total, there are seven rewards available to unlock in the Captain X series. This includes the Captain X Outfit, various key accessory items designed to go with him, and a few other miscellaneous prizes. Here are all of the available Captain X rewards you can get.

There are plenty of quests you can work on to help you get closer to unlocking Captain X. Some missions you may consider tackling next include collecting Nami’s Tangerines to help Sanji protect them, contacting Slone on the Slone Phone in Plunder Port, and using Sprite Wanted Posters to dig up and open Sprite Chests.

#3796. Footage of a Persona 1 remake has seemingly leaked online

Almost two minutes of footage from what appears to be a remake of the original Persona has leaked online.

The clip, which seemingly gives the remake the subtitle Be Your True Mind, was shared on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit. It was uploaded to file-sharing site Gofile on 31st October under a Japanese filename that translates as "Megami Ibunroku Persona Remake".

Interestingly, the footage looks a lot like Atlus' more recent entries. It shows off stylish menus and a brief look at combat that closely resembles Persona 5 and Persona 3 Reload. There's also a short social link cutscene in a noticeably different, almost graphic novel art style.

Fans digging through the clip believe they have spotted several details that lend it credibility. These include what looks like Unreal Engine debug text in the top left corner during battle (Atlus switched to Unreal Engine for Persona 3 Reload), a new remix of the original PlayStation game's Pandora theme, and the protagonist being referred to as "Boy With Earring", which is how he is named in Persona 2: Eternal Punishment.

Atlus has not announced a Persona 1 remake, and we can't verify the footage, so treat all of this with the usual caveats.

The total market share for physical games was 11%, with free-to-play skewing it a bit

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new survey from research firm Newzoo, "supported" by G2A, found that physical games represent upwards of 11% of games played by dedicated gamers, or even 30% of console games owned.

"Physical formats remain part of this landscape, despite predictions of their demise," writes Newzoo research director Alexis Pamboris.

The report collected responses from just over 6,000 "premium gamers" spread evenly across six markets: the US, UK, Germany, Poland, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia. The fieldwork period defined is August 2026, which would notably be some time after Sony announced that it will end support for new physical games in January 2028.

The "premium gamer" group is defined as people "aged 18-55 who play on PC or a Gen 9 console at least monthly," and have played AA or AAA titles in the last year that were purchased or played through a paid subscription like PlayStation Plus or Xbox Game Pass. The average premium gamer, it turns out, plays about 13.3 games a year.

Among many other things, the report looks at how these games were accessed. 43% were owned, 19% were accessed via subscription, and 38% were free-to-play games.

In total, 11% of the games played by these 6,000 gamers were physical. However, if you only look at the 43% of owned games – that is, games people paid for individually – the physical component is just over 25.5%.

Console-only gamers reported 14% physical for total ownership against 32% digital ownership. Again looking purely at the ownership split and ignoring subscription and free-to-play, physical copies represent 30.4% of the paid-for console games played in this survey period.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

"While this seems high, many of them were older releases and some will have been bought on disc or as a code in a box. Cartridges also remain common on Nintendo Switch," the survey says of the 11% base physical figure.

The focus on games played and owned, not just new games purchased, also helps explain why PC-only gamers reported 6% physical ownership, which is likely explained by the enthusiast retro market. GOG may have something to say about that niche.

Physical ownership is also slightly higher than the base in specific markets. The US and UK clock in at 12% physical total – or 27.9% and 26.6%, respectively, looking only at physical and digital games owned.

Free-to-play games are the largest single market, to no one's surprise, averaging 38% across all markets and platforms.

"The older group is slightly likelier to have bought games than use a subscription, as well as play games from physical media," the report explains.

This leads nicely to why people said they buy physical games. Digital ownership is skewed toward convenience – instant access, a portable library, digital discounts, and digital-only games – but physical game buyers more equally specified a few reasons.

Reasons to buy physical games were "less nuanced" among people who owned less than 75% of their games digitally (again, that physical chunk brings us close to that 25 - 30% ownership figure). These reasons included (in descending order of weight):

Sony's decision to walk away from physical games stoked fierce divide across the industry. Creators like Hideo Kojima are "really sad" to see discs phased out, and Kenzo Saruhashi, head honcho at JRPG house NIS, reckons Sony is "hearing the feedback from customers" amid still-burning backlash.

Like many executives, original PlayStation creator Ken Kutaragi backs the company's decision to end discs, calling the backlash a "mentality issue" and arguing discs aren't "economically reasonable."

However, while it may immediately cut costs or increase per-unit profit, some analysts worry the end of discs may also push younger or casual players further into mobile, free-to-play, and PC, which are already eating a larger share of what used to be a very console-flavored pie.

#3794. How to get free AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge in Phasmophobia

There are lots of ways you can customize your experience in Phasmophobia, including an array of ID Cards and Badges you can equip to highlight various achievements and events. Sometimes, these special items are given away to all players, as is the case with the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge.

ID Cards and Badges are some of the rarest and toughest items to unlock, as many of them require you to sink lots of time into checking off lengthy, complex goals. Because of this, free, easy-to-grab ones are always rather exciting additions you won’t want to miss out on, so here’s how to get the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge in Phasmophobia.

You can unlock the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge by logging onto Phasmophobia anytime during the redemption period. This is a free reward granted to all members of the community in celebration of over $200,000 being raised during Phasmophobia’s fundraiser for the American Heart Association Liive.

There are no additional steps you need to take to obtain this item, which is unusual for earning ID Cards and Badges, so it can take a bit of getting used to. Simply boot up the game, visit the board in the lobby, and select the “Accept” option on the AHA Advocate pop-up anytime before Nov. 15 to claim this reward and have it added to your collection forever.

Once you’ve got the AHA ID Card and Badge set unlocked, you can find them under the Customization tab in the lobby. If you’re having trouble finding them, here’s a full breakdown of where to look.

You can only grab the AHA Advocate ID Card and Badge until Nov. 15. #3793. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

#3792. The Dark Souls Devs Are Masters At Looney Tunes–Style Physical Comedy

I used to think that Dark Souls was a very serious game. A serious, serious game for serious, hardcore gamers. Grimdark, full of esoteric mysteries and depressing, philosophical themes. Tragedy in every sense. No hope for its characters. Any shred of light snuffed out by the encroaching shadow.

I have been delighted to learn in more recent years that this is actually wrong, and Dark Souls (and its sequels, both real and spiritual) are actually comedy games. Dark Souls is video-game Looney Tunes.

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-10-30T04:27:18.287Z

What the fuck is that?! A skeleton attached to a wheel of bones? A bonewheel? I guess?!

Yeah, that’s some of the funniest shit I’ve ever seen. It’s basically just this:

A lot of games try really hard to be funny via attempts at witty writing or quippy characters. Some succeed, some fail. But with Dark Souls (and Elden Ring, which I played a few years ago), FromSoftware proves it is is superb at something I imagine must be incredibly difficult to do in video games: physical comedy. You have to take into account player movement, enemy AI, objects getting caught on one anotherâthe delicate dance required to make a physical gag happen in a game like this takes such an expert hand. And yet, FromSoftware manages to Wile E. Coyote the player into incredible slapstick moments over and over, through clever use of environmental hazards and very smart enemy placement within them. You can’t tell me that reaching a tight corner and looking carefully around it just to see this sort of bullshit isn’t funny:

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-11-01T03:17:26.196Z

Yes, many (most) of these scenarios result in player death, which can be frustrating, but how can I be mad at dying if my death was absolutely hilarious? How can anyone at all be mad when your death animation looks this stupid?

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-09-10T01:47:56.059Z

It’s even better when it’s self-inflicted, which it so often is. Dark Souls is full of such clunky, clumsy movement that often, one wrong step will send you into the abyss, and it will be all your fault. Two nights ago, I lost over 30,000 souls because I accidentally dodge-rolled off an easy-to-traverse cliff on a corpse run. Sometimes, you just jump off ledges for no reason beyond your own incompetence:

— Rebekah Valentine (@duckvalentine.bsky.social) 2026-09-09T03:28:58.157Z

And I do think the comedy works all the betterÂ because Dark Souls is such a tragic story. Most of the good NPCs die ignobly, the evil ones either die after a hell of a struggle or become even worse, then die, and no one ever accomplishes their goals without a terrible cost or a monkey’s paw curling. ItÂ is the grimdark depression adventure that was billed to me, it’s justÂ also a sketch from early ’90s Sunday morning kids’ TV at the same time. It’s funny to fall off a cliff, it’s even funnier if you fall off because you got jump-scared by a freakin’ wheel made of a skeleton.

Whoever at FromSoftware is responsible for skeleton placement, I would love to interview you on this subject. Please contact me. Just whoever is the person who decides where skeletons go.

Three cheers, then, for the regular skeleton and the giant skeleton, the giant mosquitos, the mushroom people, those goddamn basilisks (may they rot in hell), the many zombie guys, and whatever that weird blob of dudes with spears surrounding that one statue in the painted world was. I love you all. And especially, most especially, three cheers for Bonewheels. I’m still not done with Dark Souls, and I hope I haven’t seen the last of you.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

"Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models."

Indie-oriented digital storefront Itch.io is beginning to push back against the rising flood of AI, announcing on social media that it's "deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop" and made it easier for users to filter out games made with generative AI.

A few days after Valve admitted that Steam has a problem with AI slop and game cloning, Itch.io chimed in to say it's experiencing something very similar: The number of game pages being created every day on the storefront has doubled over the past two months.

Itch.io didn't provide a reason for the phenomenon, but it's not hard to figure out: When one Bluesky asked why it was happening, Itch.io replied "take a guess," accompanied by crying and robot smilies, and then added that "the number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled."

Now it seems to be moving to action. "Just deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop," the storefront posted last night. "Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models."

The account also linked to Itch.io's guidelines on "uploading excessive amounts of automatically generated or AI-generated content," which says that while content created by generative AI "can be useful or interesting, do not use automated systems to mass produce product pages. We will consider this spam and may remove your pages from our browse and search pages."

The guidelines apply to, but are not limited to:

Like Steam, Itch.io requires developers and publishers to disclose their use of generative AI in their games. That disclosure requirement has now been expanded from game assets to "the tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories," all of which now require disclosure.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It has also added new browsing and search filters on the site, so users can exclude some or all use of generative AI.

The tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories on itchio now require completing an AI disclosure in order to edit or create your page. These join the game assets section which has required disclosure for the past 2 years.

The "No AI" tag page cuts straight to it:

Itch.io's action isn't likely to stem the tide of AI slop that's engulfing the world of gaming. Apart from the fact that it represents a very small percentage of a market dominated by Steam, the simple truth is that AI slop is easy to churn out in overwhelming quantities—that's what makes it so attractive to people who care less about creation than they do about making a few bucks on a lucky swing of the bat.

But it is action, and I think that's important: While some argue that mandatory AI disclosures have the potential to harm developers, the gen AI geyser is unquestionably doing harm right now, to users, developers, and the industry as a whole. Unless and until that changes, proactively excising the worst of the slop torrent and making it easier for gamers to avoid the mess entirely is the least that online storefronts can do.

#3789. One Of The Greatest Adventure Games Ever Is 30 Today, And It Wasn’t Made By LucasArts

During the heyday of the point-and-click adventure, there were two big names: LucasArts and Sierra. Of course Westwood and Revolution got a good few in there too, but there’s another name that all too often gets left out: Burst Studios. That’s the team behind Toonstruck, and, er, no, that was the only adventure it ever made. But damn, the Christopher Lloyd-starring mix of cartoon and FMV was a classic, and today marks the 30th anniversary of its release.

Unambiguously inspired byÂ Who Framed Roger Rabbit, which of course also starredÂ Back to the Future‘s Christopher Lloyd,Â Toonstruck was a glorious mix of hand-drawn cartoon animation and live-action video, somewhat less-than-seamlessly combined in what still felt like a technical marvel in 1996.

It’s all very meta at the start. Lloyd plays Drew Blanc (sorry), a cartoonist who is condemned to work on the saccharine Fluffy Fluffy Bun Bun Show, and is slowly losing his mind. His boss, played by Ben Stein (sorry about that, too), drags him back into work one night and demands that he create a collection of new bunnies for the show before the morning, but Lloyd can’t stop thinking about the character he wished he were working on, purple thing Flux Wildly. Then, er, he’s sucked into his TV and finds himself trapped in a cartoon city called Cutopia. Flux is there (and voiced by none other than Dan Castellaneta!), there’s an evil Count Nefarious in the nearby area of the Malevolands, and between the two lies Flux’s homeland, lunatic town Zanydu. Nefarious, voiced by the wondrous Tim Curry, is turning all cute things evil, and it’s up to Blanc and Flux to save the day.

Yes, the premise is stone-cold insane. And perfectly so. Toonstruck is a celebration of the anarchic nature of early-20th-century cartoons, and it takes the silly subject incredibly seriously. Along with the astonishing cast already mentioned, it also featured some of the best voice actors in the industry in smaller rolesâthe likes of David Ogden Stiers (MASH), Dom DeLuise (The Cannonball Run,Â An American Tail) and Jeff Bennett (Johnny Bravo himself). And their quality is paired with the animation, celebrating everything from Tex Avery to Disney with both love and irreverence.

Even the puzzles are great! Well, apart from a couple. But it was a mid-’90s adventure game, so, y’know. Also rather of its time is an incredibly uncomfortable moment in which Flux shouts out the r-slur, and there’s a peculiarly incongruent S&M scene with barnyard animals that perhaps wouldn’t make the cut today.

Infamously, there was supposed to be a sequel toÂ Toonstruck, but the original game’s development had been a deeply fraught time, and it was (undeservedly) a complete bomb on release.

Fortunately, it’s far easier to play today than it has been at most points in the previous 30 years. Previously relegated to an awkward fit in Dosbox and refusing anything after Windows XP, the game now boots beautifully via ScummVM, which is all done for you when you buy the game via Steam. It’s outrageously expensive at $20 for a three-decade-old game, but given it’s a whopping 10 hours long (huge compared to so many adventures of the time), you’ll get your money’s worth. There’s nothing else quite like it, and it deserves to be heralded alongside Day of the Tentacle andÂ Space Quest IV. Happy birthday, old friend.

At Dead Of Night 2: The Great Hugo picks up where the original game left off and reunites us with Maya as she heads off to investigate a large Tudor manor house.

"Five years later, Maya is still haunted by her experiences in Sea View Hotel," the blurb teases. "Desperate for answers she remembers the ghost box she used in the hotel, left there when she escaped.

"After searching on [auction] sites and in antique shops, she finds a similar looking device, but can’t get it to work. She contacts an old friend and counsellor, Quinn, who had helped her understand her supernatural experiences in the hotel. Quinn recognises the device and knows where they were made - by an inventor who used to live in a large Tudor manor house not far from Sea View - but warns her against trying to get it working. However, Maya ignores his advice and goes on her own investigation."

Quite how long "(very) soon" is, we don't yet know, but we'll keep you posted.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of the most regrettable casualties of EA's decision to shut down treasured RPG maker BioWare – well bellow the dozens of people who lost their jobs – was Mass Effect 5, the long-awaited sequel that was revealed in 2020. The project was canceled alongside EA's latest round of layoffs, but a coordinated social media effort to rescue it has attracted the attention and support of a BioWare veteran, studio co-founder Trent Oster.

According to his LinkedIn, Oster was director of technology at BioWare by the time the first Mass Effect came around in 2007, and his about page says he helped "establish the practices that scaled RPG development into billion-dollar franchises like Mass Effect and BioWare." He's best known as one of the key architects behind the early BioWare RPGs, including Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights, the latter of which he directed, but he's definitely had his hands in the Mass Effect series as well. That makes this tweet from him, in which he seemingly throws his support behind the Save Mass Effect movement online, particularly noteworthy.

"I love seeing all the energy around #SaveMassEffect," says Oster. "I think there is a still a great thesis for a well-funded RPG developer who can deliver. Makes me want to get some of the original band back together."

I love seeing all the energy around #SaveMassEffect I think there is a still a great thesis for a well-funded RPG developer who can deliver. Makes me want to get some of the original band back together.November 4, 2026

I think I can speak for Mass Effect fans when I say the idea of rallying the original developers behind Mass Effect 5 revival efforts is incredibly exciting, but unfortunately I also am obligated to bring you all right back down to earth. EA still owns the rights to Mass Effect, and it would be out of character for it to sell the rights to another studio. That said, the organizers behind the #SaveMassEffect movement have started a petition on Change.org that's about to cross 300,000 signatures, and a separate petition from the same group seeking acknowledgment from the Canadian government just today reached a major milestone.

Whether Mass Effect 5 comes back from the dead or not, Oster isn't taking EA's shutdown of evidence that big-budget RPGs are going the way of the dodo. Quite the opposite, actually, as he seemingly agrees with a commenter arguing that there's an "RPG resurgence" happening right now. "Seeing BG3 sales numbers may have had an effect," Oster says about the current state of RPG development.

The Mass Effect series is "more valuable than Dragon Age," BioWare veteran says, and it's all thanks to its worldbuilding

This week, Bethesda Game Studios is celebrating its 40th birthday—a celebration that included the full name reveal of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, successfully completing the eight-year task of adding a word to a thing.

In addition, Bethesda is commemorating the occasion with the launch of a 40th anniversary site collecting the anecdotes and favorite memories of studio staff, including one Alan Nanes. Now a design director, Nanes was originally hired at Bethesda as one of its first full-time QA testers—and by his own description, he got the job by being a pleasant fellow to spend time with.

According to Nanes, his history with Bethesda started during Morrowind's development. He was close friends with Bethesda devs in multiple departments, and it was an era where that was enough to get you in the building.

"Things were a bit 'Wild West' back then, and my friends allowed me to hang out (yes, before I was an employee) there, playing multiplayer games with them and just getting to know everyone," Nanes wrote. "Eventually, Todd Howard noticed my presence in the studio and asked if I wanted to test out their new game."

In time, his impromptu testing sessions started attracting an audience of Bethesda developers who would pick his brain about their design choices, scribble notes, and debate with each other about potential tweaks to the game while watching over his shoulder.

"It was an extraordinary feeling, the first time I felt like I was contributing to the creation of an actual videogame (I believe you can find my name in the Morrowind manual's credits under 'Special Thanks')," Nanes said. "After this became a regular occurrence, Todd Howard and Ashley Cheng seemed to decide having full-time, in-studio QA would be a valuable addition to the team, and I took on that mantle."

Nanes later graduated to a quest designer position for Oblivion, and was more recently credited as lead companions designer on Starfield. But while his tenure at Bethesda might've had a storybook trajectory, the history of QA workers at the studio has been a contentious one in the years since Nanes was hired.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Driven by frustrations surrounding compensation, advancement opportunities, workload, and more, QA workers at Bethesda's parent company ZeniMax initiated a unionization vote in 2022, officially forming ZeniMax Workers United - CWA—then the largest videogame union in the US—when the vote succeeded in January 2023.

Those frustrations remained unaddressed as contract negotiations with Microsoft stalled for over two years, driving the QA union to vote overwhelmingly in favor of authorizing a strike in April 2025. Its contract was ultimately ratified in June 2025. When a number of those QA workers were affected by Xbox's July 2026 layoffs, that contract allowed the union to enter into an "effects bargaining" process to negotiate severance terms for its impacted members, culminating in "a significant agreement" in September 2026.

#3784. Last Night’s VisionQuest Reveal Has A Whole Lot Of Marvel History Tied Up In It

VisionQuest has been pulling from a lot of the Marvel Cinematic Universeâs history, especially as it gets into the origins of artificial intelligence in the movies and delves into Visionâs relationship with his family. But last nightâs penultimate episode brought a character into the fold that some folks might not realize has some pretty significant history in the comic books as he was the first Human Torch, long before Johnny Storm took on the name in the Fantastic Four comics. Itâs time for a quick Marvel history lesson.

In the show, Paul Bettany plays J.I.M., also known as the Synthetic Man, and believe it or not, this guy is technically the first Marvel superhero, dating back to the first comic released under the brand in 1939. The character made his first appearance in the MCU in a brief cameo in Captain America: The First Avenger way back in 2011, but VisionQuest was the first time he had a proper speaking role. In the MCU, the Synthetic Man is the first of all synthetic life, and has become a cautionary tale for modern-day synthezoids like Vision because of the way he erupted into flame upon experiencing human-like emotion. He was created by Phineas Horton, who sought to rebuild his deceased son as an android, though his fixation on doing so lost him his family and fortune.Â

Their story has some more tragic consequences we wonât get into here, but the important bit here is that the Synthetic Man is the basis of all synthetic life in the MCU, and thatâs why Vision has traces of him in his code, and why they share the same face. Vision notes that J.I.M. âwears [his] face,â to which the Synthetic Man responds, âNo, you wear mine.âÂ

Though itâs not an exact adaptation of the comics, Vision and the Synthetic Man have a connection in the original story, as Vision was originally created from a copy of the androidâs body. However, because Visionâs creation differs in the MCU, with him being created from a robot body using the Mind Stone, this feels like Marvel bringing that connection back in a new way.

VisionQuest makes a point to never refer to him by his original superhero alias, which was, as many Marvel fans might not realize, the Human Torch. Most people know that as the superhero alias of Johnny Storm, one of the members of the Fantastic Four, an association strengthened by time and frequent appearances throughout modern Marvel media, leaving the android who held that mantle decades prior largely forgotten. VisionQuest hones in on the Synthetic Manâs inability to control his flames, but in the comics, he gains control of this power and uses it for good as a hero working alongside the likes of Namor and Captain America.Â

It remains to be seen if the Synthetic Man will play any major role in the MCU moving forward, but thatâs something we can speculate on further after next weekâs series finale premieres on November 10.
